abstract: |
  Approximately 1.5 million km$^2$ of land globally was converted from agriculture to highly developed areas between 1992 and 2018. The processes leading to this conversion are variable, but most farmland protection policy focuses on controlling urban sprawl. A better understanding of the multiple contexts in which farmland loss occurs can inform diverse and targeted policies for agricultural land protection. To identify multiple contexts of agricultural change, we used a mixed methods archetypes approach that identifies recurring patterns of variables in social-ecological systems across different spaces and time periods. We combined finite Gaussian mixture model cluster analysis of longitudinal quantitative data and deductive/inductive analysis of qualitative data to find recurring patterns of change over time in an agricultural land loss hotspot in the western United States [US]. Our study area included 26 counties in southern Idaho's Snake River Plain, a region with both high agricultural production and high population growth where agricultural lands are at risk of conversion. We used data from the US Census, land use/land cover spatial data, the US Census of Agriculture, and other public data sources from 1990, 2000, 2010, and 2020 to describe aspects of these counties’ natural resources, resource users, and other actors, in alignment with Ostrom’s social-ecological systems framework. We found that these 26 counties clustered into 5 resource-related groups and 5 actor-related groups. Strong determinants of a county's resource cluster were the extent of its developed lands and its housing density, whereas strong determinants of a county's actor cluster were its population density and its degree of geographical isolation. We then selected three counties for qualitative analysis of interview data and linked those insights with the results of the quantitatively derived clusters. Through combined quantitative and qualitative approaches, we found that agricultural land loss occurs in multiple contexts, including different settings along the rural-urban continuum and in more rural areas with recreation access. We reveal spatially distant counties in the same archetype that may be able to share successful farmland protection policies, as well as neighboring counties in different archetypes that will likely require different policy pathways to protect farmland. We intentionally used publicly available data so that this approach could be applied to many areas grappling with agricultural land loss.

# Introduction

Approximately 1.5 million km$^2$ of land globally has been converted from agriculture to urban and highly developed areas between 1992 and 2018, amounting to 7.5% of total global land cover change in that 25-year period [@radwan2021]. The pathway to conversion is often attributed to urban or suburban sprawl [@chen2020; @vanvliet2017], and land use projections for future agricultural land loss are based on the assumption that population growth will drive urban development of agricultural lands based on their proximity to an urban center [@xie2023; @chen2020; @haney2015]. Other pathways to agricultural land conversion, such as housing development in rural settlements and increased local commodity processing [@ju2018; @jiang2019], are not described by spatially-explicit patterns and are not operationalized in spatial land use prediction models. Thus, the focus on using urban sprawl to predict farmland loss, while other important drivers that are not spatially explicit are not used, leads to mismatches between the identification of threatened farmlands, policy implemented to protect farmland, and actual farmland conversion. For example, urban growth boundaries are effective in containing development in some small cities but ineffective in others [@dempsey2013]. To enact effective policies that protect high quality agricultural lands, it is critical to understand the multiple pathways by which those lands are converted to other uses and where they are occurring. 
<!-- Even when other pathways to agricultural land loss impact a smaller land area compared to urban sprawl, they can have significant negative impacts on local ecology and crop production [@zhu2022] and social and community well-being [@smith2001]. -->

There are three recurring patterns of farmland loss that have been described in a number of case studies: urban/suburban sprawl, amenity migration, and agricultural industrialization. First, urban sprawl is a widely recognized cause of agricultural land loss, often described by land rent or "growth machine" middle range theories [@meyfroidt2018]. As the population in urban centers grows, there is increased need for housing. While cities may create denser housing in the urban center to accommodate a larger population, they often expand outwards, creating spacious suburban neighborhoods [@dieleman2004]. As suburbs encroach on agricultural land, farmland fragmentation makes farming more difficult and encourages further development [@latruffe2014; @qiu2015; @freedgood2020]. Rising land values near urban areas are a critical barrier to entry for young farmers, which is particularly problematic with a nationwide aging farming population looking to retire [@kuethe2014; @sheridan2007]. Farmland fragmentation and rising land values create a higher likelihood that near-urban farmlands will be sold for development rather than continuing in agriculture. High quality croplands are especially susceptible to urban sprawl as both farming and housing development are easiest on flat lands with more access to freshwater [@halperin2023; @bren2017]. Demographically, urbanized areas have higher population density and diversified employment opportunities compared to more rural areas, and suburban areas in particular are linked to higher education quality and lower levels of poverty [@dumont2023; @burdick2017]. There are a number of adaptations that farmers in urbanizing areas have deployed to prevent farmland loss, including building social capital with non-farmers, diversifying operations, succession planning, and utilizing policy instruments like agricultural easements and zoning [@sharp2003; @inwood2012; @bengston2004]. Yet, few farmers in these areas expect that their farm will adequately cover their living expenses as well as production costs, sometimes even after implementing these strategies [@bruce2025]. Though urban and suburban sprawl are a prominent force in agricultural land loss and are accounted for in many land use change models focused on agricultural lands [@xie2023; @chen2020; @haney2015], the extent of this change must be understood so that farmers facing similar pressures and their policy-making representatives can learn from each others' successful and unsuccessful adaptations.

The second main driver of agricultural land loss is industrial development, often described by the "technology treadmill" middle range theory [@meyfroidt2018]. Agricultural change in the industrial context manifests differently than in urban sprawl. In the United States, food manufacturing occurs in both urban and rural areas, especially those with access to raw materials (e.g. milk), labor availability, favorable policies, and sufficient infrastructure, including major interstate roadways, water, and electricity [@lambert2009; @compton2018]. Additionally, the presence of one manufacturing facility is correlated with the presence of other facilities, as well as with associated commodity production [@lambert2009]. Besides conversion of agricultural land for manufacturing facilities, these factories can attract non-local workers who need housing, yet their settlement patterns may be different from those of urban sprawl populations. For example, rapid Hispanic population growth is associated with food processing plants in rural America [@lichter2012]. To adapt to an industrializing agricultural economy, farmers near food processing plants can increase their sales by increasing their production of raw materials for their specific local industry, but this comes at considerable input and labor costs [@jafri2024]. Thus, industrial development involves different demands for land and farmer adaptations compared to urban sprawl.

<!-- Across Asia, conversion of agricultural land to industry use precedes urban sprawl or occurs alongside urban sprawl [@azadi2011; @tuyen2013; @zhou2020]. In Europe, a large portion of manufacturing was shifted to rural areas in the late 1970s [@keeble1983], and food manufacturing is an important component of many rural economies [@rizov2011]. -->

The third major pathway to rural land change is amenity migration, i.e. the migration of urban dwellers to rural areas for specific lifestyle amenities [@abrams2012], described by middle range theories such as rural gentrification [@gosnell2011]. Rural sprawl associated with amenity migration tends to be less dense than urban sprawl, resulting in larger areas of land affected, but with less intensity and sometimes further from population centers [@radeloff2005; @hammer2004]. Amenity migrants with agricultural estates do not rely on agricultural production as a means of income; though they may engage in some form of farming (including hobby farms) or lease lands to local producers, they may also use their lands exclusively for non-production uses like recreation and conservation [@abrams2012; @abrams2013; @matarrita2025]. Local jobs in areas with amenity migration are primarily low-wage service jobs, and this combined with rising property values can push low-income households farther out of the high-amenity community [@sherman2018; @loeffler2007; @abrams2012]. Thus, agricultural producers may face rising land costs and falling off-farm wages, the need to lease land, and the fragmentation of agricultural lands by migrant estates and commuter roads. Amenity migrants also change the cultural and political makeup of the communities in which they relocate by bringing different expectations and values [@abrams2012]. Clashing expectations can create tension between producers and migrants, yet farmers also may find receptive collaborators in amenity migrants who want to keep lands in agriculture [@matarrita2025; @abrams2013]. Amenity migration is a distinct pathway to agricultural land loss that differs in cause and effects from urban sprawl and industrial expansion, and requires different policy and planning approaches to address.

Since agricultural land conversion occurs via distinct processes in distinct spatiotemporal contexts, farmland loss may be well described by archetype analysis. Archetypes are recurring patterns of social-ecological variables that build towards middle-range theories -- generalizations that describe causal pathways within a well-bounded range of phenomena [@meyfroidt2018; @oberlack2019].  Archetype analyses may use quantitative, qualitative, or mixed methods, and often use multiple models to capture diversity within cases of a phenomenon, rather than using a single model to explain all relationships between processes and outcomes [@oberlack2019; @sietz2019]. For example, @magliocca2019 constructed 12 multi-component archetypes of land use change outcomes stemming from economic land concessions by combining a quantitative survival analysis and a qualitative comparative analysis of case studies. An emerging application of archetype analysis is dynamic archetype analysis, which not only identifies recurring social-ecological patterns across space but also through time [@orozco2024]. While dynamic archetype analysis could be very useful to illuminate farmland loss dynamics, it has not yet been applied in this context.

The overarching goal of this research is to identify and describe archetypes, or recurring patterns, of agricultural land loss, which will aid in identifying where distinct processes of land use change are occurring and will contribute to a diverse toolbox for agricultural lands protection in diverse localities. The Snake River Plain of Idaho is an ideal place to study multiple processes of farmland loss because it is experiencing different drivers of agricultural land conversion across its counties. Based on in-depth knowledge of the study area, we hypothesized that land use change is occurring in different areas across the region, due to three different processes described in the farmland loss literature: urban/suburban sprawl, agricultural industrialization, and amenity migration. We then tested this hypothesis with an archetype analysis that combines quantitative clustering analysis and qualitative deductive/inductive analysis of semi-structured interviews within focal communities of the study area. Our research questions were:

1. Are there recurrent combinations of social-ecological indicators, i.e. archetypes, in Idaho's Snake River Plain, and how have they changed over time?
2. What is the relationship between these archetypes and farmland loss, and do the archetypes identify cases of urban sprawl, amenity migration, and industrialization?
3. In what ways do actors in select counties describe drivers of community change, and do these insights validate archetypes indicating urban sprawl, industrialization, or amenity migration?

# Methods

## Study Area

The Snake River Plain ecoregion of the United States [@ecoregions] intersects with 26 counties in the state of Idaho (109,700 km$^2$). It contains  productive croplands [@freedgood2020], localized yet rapidly growing highly developed urban areas [@census_metro], and public rangelands grazed by livestock (@freedgood2020). This region features two primary ecological zones, the river plain and the shrub steppe, and a diverse range of social systems, from urban and exurban systems to dryland agriculture and rural public lands, that together form a diverse array of social-ecological systems [@aho2022]. 

Farmland protection in southern Idaho is based on the 1981 Right to Farm section of Idaho Code, which protects farmlands from nuisance lawsuits [@IDRightToFarm], and the 1975 Local Land Use Planning Act, which mandates that cities and counties must plan and zone [@IDLLUPA; @meyer2025]. Therefore, farmland protection actions and funding from 1990-2020 in southern Idaho occur at the county level or lower. Farmland protection is mainly accomplished through zoning that prevents development on farmland or, rarely, costly perpetual easements established in partnership with land trusts or local government [@pald]. Before 2020, Idaho's Snake River Plain contained 64 agricultural easements totaling 271 $km^2$, or 0.2% of the total study area [@pald].

## Data Selection

The social-ecological systems [SES] framework first published in 2007 by Elinor Ostrom is a conceptual framework that provides a list of variables that may affect the outcome of a SES [@ostrom2009; @partelow2018]. For comparative analysis of multiple case studies, it provides structure and variables for comparison [@oberlack2016; @partelow2018]. The framework introduces variables describing four major subsystems in a SES: resource systems, resource units, governance systems, and actors, as well as variables describing the interactions of these systems, the related ecosystem, and the social, economic, and political setting [@ostrom2009]. Readily-available public data can describe some of these systems comprehensively, while it is difficult to quantify indicators for others [@partelow2018]. We chose to focus on three subsystems: the resource system and resource units, which we combine into a single resource model, and the actors. We assume the fourth subsystem, governance, is fairly similar across the study area, since all counties have a similar county government structure and adhere to the same state and national laws. We linked data available from 1990-2020 to second-tier variables in these subsystems of the SES framework based on expert knowledge from the authors. Some second-tier variables are excluded because no relevant data sources could be found, but it is common to analyze subsets of SES variables in the SES literature [@partelow2018]. We scaled all data by mean normalization [@hennig2016]. Detailed data sources and processing steps for each indicator and year can be found in Appendix A.

##  Cluster Analysis

Cluster analysis is a common method for archetype identification [@sietz2019], particularly the heuristic method of k-means clustering initialized by hierarchical clustering [@kok2016; @sietz2017; @vidal2019]. K-means uses Euclidean distance to cluster points around a centroid [@patel2020]. However, this calculation method is limited in its ability to find complex data structures, as it assumes that data clusters will be spherical with equal volume [@patel2020; @scrucca2023]. Complex systems may be better described by generative model-based clustering, which describes each cluster as a probability distribution, allowing for a variety of cluster shapes (i.e. spheres and ellipses) and cluster volumes in dimensional space [@scrucca2023]. Specifically, Gaussian mixture model-based clustering, which describes each cluster as a mixture of Gaussian probability distributions, is a flexible and popular method for clustering continuous variables [@scrucca2023]. 

We fit two separate Gaussian mixture models, one with the resource variables and one with the actor variables, in order to characterize the resource and actor subsystems of the counties separately. We treated each county-year combination (e.g. Ada County in 1990) as a single observation, for a total of 104 observations.

### Model Selection

There are three components to model selection in Gaussian-based cluster modeling: variable selection, number of clusters, and cluster shape. First, variable selection is used to remove redundant or irrelevant variables from the data that could degrade the performance of model-based clustering [@bouveyron2019]. Reducing the dimensions of the data reduces the number of parameters needed to specify the covariance matrices of the clustering models, some of which require up to $d^2$ parameters per cluster, where $d$ is the dimension of the data [@bouveyron2019; @scrucca2023]. Dimension reduction is important in this analysis because we have relatively few observations (n=104) compared to dimensions (30 resource variables, 19 actor variables), and we cannot estimate more model parameters than observations. We can test more combinations of cluster shape and number of clusters that require more parameters if we reduce the number of dimensions [@scrucca2023; @bouveyron2019]. While all of our chosen indicators convey important information about an agricultural social-ecological system, we decided to remove redundant indicators in order to test more clustering configurations.

We identified redundant indicators by systematically checking single variables for exclusion using a backward stepwise greedy search, which allowed us to take variable dependencies into account [@bouveyron2019; @clustvarsel]. We began with the full set of variables, then tested the exclusion of each indicator individually, dropping the single most redundant variable, as identified by BIC. Then, this step was repeated with the remaining indicators until all indicators were identified as useful for clustering. At all steps after the first, we tested the inclusion of all dropped variables and added any that showed new evidence for clustering importance after other variables were dropped. We used the R package `clustvarsel` for variable selection (v2.3.5, @clustvarsel).

The next two steps of model selection are selecting the shape of the clusters in dimensional space (e.g. spherical vs elliptical) and the number of clusters, both of which we implemented with R package `mclust` [v6.1.1, @scrucca2023]. We tested for a range of 1-5 clusters in each model, as it is recommended to vary the number of possible clusters between 1 and the next integer after $n^{0.3}$ [4 < 104$^{0.3}$ < 5, @biernacki2006]. We tested only spherical and diagonal models to limit to model structures with less possible parameters than observations (see @scrucca2023 for a description of all possible shapes).

Because clustering models are sensitive to their initialization, we ran each model 200 times with random initialization. We selected the best model structure of the 200 runs using BIC, and the log likelihoods for the 200 runs of both models indicated no evidence of alternative local solutions [@bauer2021].

### Selected Model Structures

In the resource model, the following indicators were redundant: (1) land in farms, (2) percent cropland, (3) percent federal land, (4) percent non-federal land near a major roadway, (5) distance to a national park, (6) accommodation and food service jobs, (7) percent change in farms, (8) percent change in cropland, and (9) the second principal component for farm size. The optimal number of clusters was 5, and the optimal cluster shape was EVI [diagonal distribution, with equal volume, variable shape, and orientation on the coordinate axes in dimensional space, @scrucca2023].

In the actors model, the following indicators were redundant: (1) the second principle componant of employment, (2) percent retired, (3) average age, (4) median household income, (5-6) both education levels, high school and Bachelor's degree, (7) racial composition, (8) farm tenure, and (9) percent farms with net loss. The optimal number of clusters was 5, and the optimal cluster shape was EVI [diagonal distribution, with equal volume, variable shape, and orientation on the coordinate axes in dimensional space, @scrucca2023].

To determine the most influential variables in each model, we used dimension reduction to maximally separate clusters, similar to principle component analysis [@scrucca2023]. We multiplied the contribution of each indicator to each reduced dimension by the overall explanatory power of each dimension, then summed each variable's contributions. We used this value to identify the variables that were most important for creating the most separated clusters.

A data-driven methodological routine to identify key indicators for social-ecological system archetype mapping. Environmental Research Letters, 17(4), 045019. -->

## Qualitative Analysis

Qualitative data were collected in Idaho's Snake River Plain from 2023 to 2026. Our efforts were concentrated in the Treasure, Magic, and Teton Valleys, where we identified distinct drivers of farmland loss prior to the creation of the quantitative clusters: urban sprawl in Treasure Valley (Canyon County), agricultural industrialization in Magic Valley (Twin Falls County), and natural amenity migration in Teton Valley (Teton County). We conducted in-depth interviews and over 150 hours of participant observation. Using a semi-structured guide, we completed 37 interviews with 22 farmers and ranchers, policy actors, and other farmland protection advocates. Interview durations ranged from 51 to 196 minutes (average 75 minutes). All interviews were audio recorded and transcribed verbatim.  Here we present results on the most common drivers of community change. The names given to each archetype were informed by these data and the research team’s local expertise.

var_labs_A <- data.frame(indicator = colnames(clust_dat$Actors)[order(colnames(clust_dat$Actors))],

## Cluster Descriptions

### Resource Clusters

The most influential variables in the resource model were housing density and developed land (@suppfigb-R-influential).

<!-- comment to ask: re-level in order of influence rather than methods tables? TTC says yes -->

```{r}
#| label: fig-R-CIs
#| message: false
#| fig-cap: "Characteristics of each Resource cluster. The resource cluster model determined the mean for each variable in each cluster, and we used bootstrapping to obtain 95% confidence intervals [@scrucca2023]. Since variables were scaled between -1 and 1, if the confidence interval contains 0, the variable mean is not significantly different ($p>0.05$) than the overall mean across the study area (the Snake River Plain) and time period (1990-2020). These variables are shown in gray. Variables with significantly different means, suggesting that they are distinctive characteristics of that cluster, are shown in black."
#| fig-height: 8.5
#| fig-width: 8
  
##############
# code for model output instead of raw data

ci_clust$Resource %>%
  mutate(cluster = factor(cluster,

                          labels = c("R1", "R2", "R3", "R4", "R5"))) %>%
  mutate(input_data_name = factor(input_data_name,

ggplot(aes(x = mean, y = input_data_name, colour = sig)) +

  theme(text = element_text(size = 14),
        panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

<!-- urban amenities -> urban services and infrastructure? -->

#### Cluster R1: Flattest land, with urban services

Characteristic resources of R1 are a high extent of developed land, higher housing density, high access to highways and urban areas, more healthcare workers, and flatter land (@fig-R-CIs, @suppfigb-R-ranges). This cluster has the highest percentage of small farms of all the resource clusters (@supptblb-data-r1). These counties have experienced higher cropland loss and developed land gain compared to other resource clusters (@suppfigb-R-ranges). This cluster is home to Boise, the largest city in Idaho, and neighboring Canyon County, known for its high quality farmland but experiencing urban sprawl from the Boise metropolitan area (@fig-cluster-maps; see @sec-canyon for qualitative analysis).

#### Cluster R2: Flat lands moderately near to natural amenities and urban services

R2 is the cluster closest to the study area average for most indicators (@fig-R-CIs). Few lands are in urban areas, but ca. 66% are within 30 miles of an urban area while ca. 33% are further than 30 miles from urban services (@supptblb-data-r2). Farm density is slightly lower than average, with 43% small farms, 34% medium farms, and 22% large farms, on average (@fig-R-CIs, @supptblb-data-r2). Median home values are also slightly lower than average. This is one of three clusters with slightly less developed land gain and cropland loss, yet cropland loss rates are quite variable within counties and years in this cluster (@suppfigb-R-ranges). This cluster contains twelve counties (@fig-cluster-maps). An illustrative example of this cluster is Twin Falls County, which contains the growing city of Twin Falls and a growing dairy industry, fueled by the recent establishment of a large yogurt processing plant (see @sec-twinfalls for qualitative analysis).

#### Cluster R3: Flat lands near urban services with more agriculture

Cluster R3 has less presence of natural land covers like forest and shrublands, and higher than average cover of cropland and developed land (@fig-R-CIs, @suppfigb-R-ranges). Though there are many rivers, access to other natural amenities such as lakes, forests, and recreation lands are low (@suppfigb-R-ranges). Like R2, there is not much urban land in these counties, but almost all of their lands are within 30 miles of an urban area (@supptblb-data-r3). On average, over half the lands of these counties are part of farms, but developed land gain is the second highest after R1 (@supptblb-data-r5, @fig-R-CIs). This cluster contains four counties (@fig-cluster-maps).

<!-- Because counties in this archetype have a considerable amount of agricultural lands and are moderately close to cities but do not contain cities themselves, they may be candidates for both agricultural industrialization, or amenity migration for migrants who are specifically seeking a rural agricultural setting. -->

#### Cluster R4: Mountain recreation moderately near urban services

Characteristic resources of R4 are a greater presence of forestland and more steep lands (@fig-R-CIs). These counties are closer to ski areas and have a higher presence of recreation land, have an average presence of lakes and rivers, and support more jobs in hospitality (@fig-R-CIs, @supptblb-data-r4). There is less developed or urban land, more federal land, and both housing and farm density are low for the study area (@fig-R-CIs, @suppfigb-R-ranges). However, most of the land in these counties lie within 30 miles of an urban area and its services (@supptblb-data-r4). These counties have the highest home values compared to other clusters (@fig-R-CIs, @supptblb-data-r4). Rates of cropland loss and developed land gain are fairly low compared to other clusters (@suppfigb-R-ranges). This cluster contains six counties (@fig-cluster-maps). An illustrative example is Teton County, which attracts outdoor recreationists to live in its small towns and rural areas (see @sec-teton for qualitative analysis).

#### Cluster R5: Range- and public lands far from urban services

The unique characteristics of R5 are more shrubland cover, less cropland cover, a greater amount of federal land, greater distance from urban areas, and less access to highways (@fig-R-CIs, @suppfigb-R-ranges, @supptblb-data-r5). Natural amenities are also few, with less river miles, lower lake area, average presence of recreation and forest land, and long distances to a ski areas (@fig-R-CIs). Similar to R2, R5 has more large farms and less farms operating at a loss (@supptblb-data-r5). R5 has low rates of cropland loss and developed land gain, and it is also losing fewer farms than other counties (@suppfigb-R-ranges). This cluster contains three counties (@fig-cluster-maps).

### Actors Clusters

The most influential variables in the resource model were: (1) population density and (2) geographic isolation (@suppfigb-A-influential).

#### Cluster A1: Urban counties with high population growth

The defining characteristics of A1 are its high population density and urban population, with most people living and working in metropolitan or micropolitan counties (counties containing urban areas with population >50,000 or 10,000-49,999, respectively; @fig-A-CIs, @supptblb-data-a1). A1 also has high population growth, higher incomes, and a higher percentage of residents with a Bachelor's degree (@suppfigb-A-ranges). Despite a lower proportion of residents in agricultural production, the number of hired agricultural workers is high for the study area, indicating the high production needs of the farms that remain in these counties (@supptblb-data-a1, @fig-A-CIs). The share of farms that are fully owned by the producer is slightly higher than any other actors archetype, and these counties also have higher percentages of farms operating at a loss. These farm labor, tenure, and profit rates indicate that farming in these counties is financially challenging.

#### Cluster A2: Small cities 

In cluster A2, population density and growth are average for the study area and most residents live in a micropolitan (within an urban area with population 10,000-49,999) or a non-urban census block (@fig-A-CIs, @supptblb-data-a2). Most residents live and work in the same county, though some travel to other micropolitan areas, and the sectors with the highest employment are healthcare/social services and retail trade (@supptblb-data-a2). Median income and percentage of residents with a Bachelor's degree as the highest degree attained are the second highest of the clusters, after A1.

#### Cluster A3: Small city with university

Cluster A3, comprised of a single county (@fig-cluster-maps), is similar to cluster A2 in that it is comprised of mostly micropolitan and non-urban census blocks, but is distinguished by its higher population density and growth and its education and employment demographics. In A3, most residents have attained a higher educational level than high school or a Bachelor's degree, and a high percentage (37%) are employed in education. Madison County contains the small city of Rexburg and Brigham Young University - Idaho, which influences the demographics and population dynamics of this county enough to create its own cluster in our study area.

#### Cluster A4: Small town counties

Most residents in A4 counties live in non-urban census blocks, with the remaining 23-53% of residents living in census blocks in small towns (within urban areas of population <9,999; @supptblb-data-a4). Population density is low, though population growth is average (@fig-A-CIs). Agricultural and other primary producers make up a higher percentage of the working population, along with retail trade and manufacturing (@supptblb-data-a4).

#### Cluster A5: Geographically isolated rural counties

A5 contains counties with no urban areas, low population density, and average population growth (@fig-A-CIs, @supptblb-data-a5). Residents of A5 counties are the least likely to work in the same county they live in compared to other clusters; the next most used commutes in A5 are commuting to other micropolitan or small town counties (@supptblb-data-a5). The A5 cluster has the lowest median incomes and the highest employment in agriculture and other primary production industries, as well as recreation.

Development outcomes are mediated by both resource and actor archetypes (@fig-resouce-actor-combo). The most development is in R1. In both R2 and R3, actor archetypes A2 (small cities) and A4 (rural counties with more urban influence) had greater gains in developed lands than A3 (small town counties grow as quickly as small cities) and A5 (geographically isolated rural counties with less economic opportunity). In R4, development gains decrease more linearly along the actor archetype gradient of most to least urban. A1 is the actor archetype associated with high population growth and density, yet those actors' impacts on developed land gains are mediated by the resource system. A1 counties are associated with more developed land gain in R1 counties than in the R3-A1 county.

## Insights from Changing Communities

For the following results, we combine insights from longitudinal public data used to generate the quantitative archetypes (described in @tbl-datasel, A[-@supptbla-means) and qualitative data from interviews and participant observations in three key counties in different archetypes.

### Urban Sprawl in Canyon County {#sec-canyon}

Canyon County is in the resource archetype "R1: risk of urban sprawl – flat land with accessible urban amenities." It transitioned from the actor archetype "A2 - small cities" to “A1 - urban counties with high population growth" between 2000 and 2010. Canyon County experienced rapid growth from 1990 to 2020, with housing density doubling and population density tripling [@CofPopHous_1990; @cencounts; @decennial_2020]. There has been a corresponding decline in agriculture: cropland decreased by 10% and land in farms decreased by 25% in those 30 years [@nlcd; @CofAg_1992_landinfarms; @CofAg_quickstats]. The nature of farm ownership has also changed: in 1990, 52% of farms were 1-50 acres and 53% were fully owned, and in 2020, 80% of farms were 1-50 acres and 78% were fully owned [@CofAg_1992_landinfarms; @CofAg_quickstats]. Homes are also more expensive – median home values doubled from 1990 (\$108,255) to 2020 [\$211,600, @CofHous_1990; @acs2020]. Overall, these data suggest that Canyon County is a case of urban sprawl overtaking agriculture land for residential and commercial development. 

Aligning with our archetype analysis, our qualitative data for Canyon County suggests that the top perceived driver of community change is urban sprawl. Many interview participants perceived this urban development as inevitable, with agricultural land being developed without discernment. As one rancher noted, "I do see this in almost every community around us in the Treasure Valley an almost insatiable appetite for more housing without stopping." 

While zoning and planning policies could limit development, there has been little effort made to enact or enforce such policies. As noted by one farmer, "Anything that comes online, it's seen as a future development. Like, seemingly every listing doesn't just say, 'great agricultural parcel - come purchase it - expand your operation' no instead the first sentence is 'great development potential'."  There is a belief that when a farmer decides to sell their agricultural land, the market and developers will immediately assume that a rezone request out of the agricultural zone and into the residential zone will be easily acquired. This is fed by a historically 'laissez-faire' political attitude, a strong focus on private property rights primacy, and exponential demographic growth. In Canyon County, the potential for development is overriding the potential of agricultural land.

### Agricultural Industrialization in Twin Falls County {#sec-twinfalls}

Twin Falls County is in resource archetype "R2 - flat land near natural and urban amenities" and actor archetype "A2 - small cities." Though it did not undergo an archetype shift, Twin Falls County is experiencing agricultural industrialization, specialization, and concentration. Farms in Twin Falls County have changed, with a declining "agriculture of the middle." In 1992 there were 762 farms between 50-500 acres, while in 2022 there were 351. There was an increase in both small and large farms over the same period, with 1-50 acre farms increasing from 495 to 673 and farms over 2,000 acres increasing from 34 to 46 [@CofAg_1992_landinfarms; @CofAg_quickstats]. Developed land has increased from 3% to 5% of the county [@nlcd], but agricultural land has declined very little. In 2020, there was 3% less cropland and 5% less land in farms compared to 1990 [@nlcd; @CofAg_1992_landinfarms; @CofAg_quickstats]. The population has increased from 53,580 in 1990 to 90,046 in 2020, yet employment in agriculture has remained around 5% [@cencounts; @decennial_2020; @cbp1997; @cbp2022; @CofAg_quickstats]. Some urban growth is evidenced by expanding service industries, with increasing employment in healthcare and hospitality [@cbp1997; @cbp2022]. Overall, these data suggest that Twin Falls County is a case of agricultural industrialization fueling modest urban growth. However, should growth persist as our overall actor archetype trajectories suggest, farmland loss in Twin Falls may become uncontrolled and jeopardize the stability and viability of the agribusiness economy driving the county’s economic and demographic change. 

Interview data in Twin Falls County suggests that agricultural industrialization is perceived to be the main driver of community and land use change, aligning with the archetype analysis. Interview participants observed that agribusinesses are expanding to the point of changing both the physical and socio-cultural landscape of Twin Falls. Physical shifts include an expansion of industrial agricultural facilities. As one resident noted, "Everybody now is within a stone's throw of some dairy facility of some kind." Respondents also discussed the increase in urbanization. This is reflected in the statement from a lifelong resident of the valley and self-identified "farm kid", who noted that "the demographic of Twin Falls has changed from a little tiny cowtown to a pretty urban area."

Agricultural industrialization was viewed as not only shifting the physical landscape, but the cultural and social landscape as well. One respondent explained that "in the last two years the number of out of state plates has changed from just California/Nevada, [...] to Kansas, to Texas, to Missouri, the Midwest. [...] it's because the recruiters from these [agribusiness] companies are going far and wide to find the workers." The perceived social and cultural shifts within the community have generated conflicts related to land use. Notably, the valley has become 'too good at agribusiness', to the extent that incoming residents employed within the industry are increasingly acquiring agricultural land for residential and commercial development, thereby fueling urban expansion. While urbanization has encroached on farmland and shifted the physical and cultural landscape, respondents still saw the area as agricultural. As one respondent told us, "[Twin Falls] is still dependent on agriculture." Twin Falls County’s continued dependence on agriculture while undergoing farmland loss is a perfect example of the tension unique to the agricultural industrialization archetype.

### Amenity Migration in Teton County {#sec-teton}

Teton County is in resource archetype "R3 - access to mountain recreation and urban amenities." It transitioned from actor archetype "A5 - geographically isolated rural counties with less economic opportunity" to "A4 - rural counties with more urban influence." Teton County is located near mountains and recreation areas, including nearby ski areas and national parks. It does not contain a densely populated urban area; the closest urban center is 20-40 miles away [@ipums]. Though it maintains its rural nature in this regard, Teton County is also undergoing rapid change. The population remains scattered, but both population and housing density have more than tripled from 1990 to 2020 [@CofPopHous_1990; @cencounts; @decennial_2020]. Median home values have also almost tripled in that time, from \$122,494 to \$358,100 [@CofHous_1990; @acs2020]. In those 30 years, developed land has increased from 3% to 5% of the county [@nlcd], and employment trends reflect a shift towards both housing development and a recreation economy. Jobs in agriculture have declined from 22% to 12% from 1997 to 2022, while there are increases in construction (8% to 20%), hospitality (8% to 14%), and recreation (2% to 3%) jobs [@cbp1997; @cbp2022; @CofAg_quickstats]. Overall, these data suggest that Teton County is experiencing amenity migration.

Our qualitative data also suggests that the top perceived driver of community change is amenity migration. "Most of the people I knew moved here for fishing, for skiing, or hunting, for outdoor recreation." This quote by an 'old-newcomer' who moved to the valley in the early 1990s, echoes a common sentiment among respondents that most of the population growth has been fueled by outdoor enthusiasts and growth in the outdoor economy. 

This amenity migration growth has led to land values skyrocketing. Under these new market conditions farmers are no longer competing for land among themselves, but against wealthy outdoor recreationists and speculative developers seeing promise in the valley’s outdoor economy. One multigenerational farmer we spoke with said that they haven’t been able to expand their land base because "[they]'ve got corporate people buying ground just on speculation" and inflating agricultural land values. Farmland becoming too expensive for agricultural use has made it difficult for new and established farmers alike to grow their operations. As a response, they sometimes exit farming entirely and those farmlands are developed along the amenity migration process.

## Cluster Transitions {#sec-transitions}

There was one resource transition in the study period: Power County transitioned from R3 (Access to mountain recreation and urban amenities) to R2 (Flat land near natural and urban amenities) in 2000 (@fig-cluster-maps). This can be attributed to a lower percentage of residents employed in hospitality, as well as less large farms and less cropland loss after 2000.

Looking across actor transitions, we can put together a common progression through actor archetypes. The most rural and isolated archetype is A5 (geographically isolated rural counties with less economic opportunity). From A5, counties transition to A4 (rural counties with more urban influence), keeping their rural nature but transitioning away from traditional rural careers, or they transition to A3 (small town counties grow as quickly as small cities), if population growth is concentrated and creates an urban area. A4 may further transition to A3 if an urban area is created (i.e. Gem County, 1990 to 2000). Next, A3 counties transition to A2 (small cities) once enough population growth has occurred to reclassify the small towns in A3 counties to the micropolitan areas of A2 counties. Finally, A2 counties may become even more urbanized A1 counties if enough population growth occurs and/or occupations reflect a more urban setting (e.g. a higher share of employment in education; @fig-cluster-maps).

# Discussion

## Archetype analysis links spatially and temporally separated but thematically similar counties

This analysis recontextualizes counties in the study area, linking counties that are spatially separated but have similar resources and actors. For example, Twin Falls County and Bingham County are both R2-A2 in 2020 -- small cities with flat land near natural and urban amenities. The archetype shift in Bingham County occurred between 2000-2010, indicating that they will face similar agricultural changes and risks of farmland conversion to Twin Falls, but at a delayed rate. Bingham County may be able to learn from farmland protection interventions in Twin Falls. Unfortunately, our qualitative data suggests that farmland protection has been extremely limited in Twin Falls. Instead of suggesting transferable policies, we propose that Bingham County should consider its possible "no policy implemented" future may look similar to Twin Falls, and decide if they would like to implement policies that guide their county's future in a different direction. Another example is Teton County and Minidoka County, which are both in actor archetype A4 -- rural counties with more urban influence. Though they are in different resource archetypes, they are both dealing with agricultural and community change stemming from population growth. One example of this is new Latter-Day Saints temples under construction or newly completed in counties neighboring both Teton and Minidoka [@brugger2024; @wilt2025]. Ongoing qualitative data analysis is reavealing that producers and old newcomers are allied in advocating for farmland protection in Teton County [@daumale2026]. It is unclear if this alliance arises from Teton's combination of actors and resources, or if it is possible in multiple resource archetypes. If the producer-old newcomer alliance primarily arises from actor type alone, Minidoka County might pursue a similar alliance of farmland protection advocates.

Archetype analysis also revealed gaps in our knowledge that can be used for future studies of community change. In the beginning of this study, we hypothesized that we would identify archetypes related to three major phenomena that lead to farmland conversion -- urban sprawl, agricultural industrialization, and amenity migration -- and we conducted interviews and qualitative analysis in a selection of counties where these processes were occurring. However, the archetype analysis also revealed the R4 group of counties (agriculture further from urban and recreational amenities) that we had not identified as requiring targeted qualitative data collection. Local knowledge suggests that farmland conversion may be in its beginning stages in R4 counties, as farmers there are receiving cold calls about selling their land to prospective buyers (David Anderson, personal communication). This archetype will require further study to understand its unique dynamics of agricultural change.

Dynamic archetype analysis (archetype change through time) is an especially useful tool for considering multifaceted, temporal SES dynamics. Dynamic archetypes are a fairly recent innovation within the archetype analysis literature, and have primarily been used to study how a major change or "shock" to a system results in archetype change. For example, @orozco2024 used dynamic archetypes to study the effect of EU agricultural policies on agricultural changes in Germany. Our study is located in a place and time where farmland protection policy is fairly weak and has not changed. Absent major policy change, we were able to build a proposed timeline of actor archetype transitions that we expect to occur by observing all the transitions that took place in our study period (see @sec-transitions). We propose that this timeline reveals likely future scenarios that each county may face, which can inform proactive policy design. Longitudinally comparable datasets are important for this work. In this analysis, we've laid the blueprint to use public data in this way for any region in the US.

## Multiple resource archetypes are at risk of farmland loss, actor archetypes indicate likely rate of development

R1, the cluster losing the most cropland and land in farms and gaining the most developed land, contains counties that exhibit the traditional patterns of urban sprawl -- particularly Ada and Canyon Counties, which contain Idaho's largest city (Boise) and its metropolitan area. However, other archetypes (R2-R4) are also gaining developed land. These outcomes are tied not only to the resource archetype, but also the actor archetype. In both R2 and R3, the largest gains in developed land are observed when the actor archetype is urban counties with high population growth (A1), small cities (A2) or rural with more urban influence (A4). In these resource contexts, certain actor archetypes are more likely to fuel non-farm development: the growing cities and rural areas transitioning away from an agricultural economy.

Three resource archetypes at risk of farmland loss are either on flat lands with access to urban amenities (R1, R2) or near mountain recreation (R3). These results align with existing research on farmland conversion. Flat, accessible lands, such as those in R1 and R2, are prime sites for residential and commercial development as well as farming [@halperin2023], and in these resource archetypes, residential development is proceeding while cropland area declines. On the other end of the spectrum, rural areas near mountain recreation offer many natural amenities, and non-farm residential and commercial development caters to a growing population of amenity migrants [@abrams2012]. R4, agriculture further from urban and recreational amenities, also has access to urban amenities (all lands are within 50 miles of an urban area) and is experiencing various levels of development. Some of this development may reflect a newer type of amenity migration with less affluent amenity migrants [@matarrita2025].

Our finding that some actor archetypes have higher rates of development than others, particularly that growing small town counties have lower rates of development than some rural counties in R2 and R3, was more surprising. This finding highlights both the strengths and limitations of the USDA Rural-Urban Commuting Area (RUCA) codes, which we adapted for this analysis and were strong drivers of the actor archetypes. The strength of the RUCA methodology is that the urban population threshold used to distinguish between small town and micropolitan counties is useful for delineating different rates of development in R2 and R3 counties. However, our clustering identified two distinct rural actor archetypes, one of which had higher rates of development (A4) than the other (A5), that are not reflected in the "rural"  RUCA category.


## Qualitative data enriches quantitative archetypes

Qualitative data enhances archetype analysis by providing further context and validation of our findings. A limitation of the data driven archetypes is their failure to detect changes in counties without archetype shifts. Our actor archetypes were designed to reflect community change, but they are strongly tied to data on metropolitan, micropolitan, small town, and rural areas, determined by population and housing density thresholds [@ruca]. When a county remains between these thresholds, changes in its actors are not as easily detected, though it did occur once in this analysis (Madison County, a micropolitan county that became part of A1 in 2010). Twin Falls is one county that did not shift in its actor archetype, yet interview data revealed community changes while at the same time affirming its unchanged economic reliance on agricultural products. Our qualitative findings underscore the need to consider change even in places that did not switch archetypes through time.

In the rapidly expanding field of archetype analysis for sustainability science, there has been a need to establish methods for archetype validation. Robust archetypes require both internal validation to demonstrate that cases in each archetype are indeed more similar to each other than to other cases and external validation to demonstrate the extent to which the archetypes are applicable outside the study [@eisenack2019]. We contend that qualitative data collection is a method for both types of validation. In this study, we used qualitative data for limited internal validation. In this preliminary analysis of the qualitative data, we were only able to analyze data for one case each in 3 of the 5 resource and actor archetypes. These data build a fuller picture of community change in these archetypes than could be constructed with quantitative data alone. Future research may be able to use qualitative data collection in multiple cases in each archetype to reveal nuanced similarities and differences in outcomes and social-ecological attributes between cases, furthering the use of qualitative data for internal archetype validation. Qualitative data can also be used for external validation when a rich literature of case studies exists for similar phenomena outside the study area. For example, amenity migration in the western United States is a well studied phenomenon in rural sociology. Based on numerous case studies, we believe the R3 archetype is valid in areas near mountains across the western United States [@sherman2018; @abrams2013]. Linking quantitative data, qualitative data, and published case studies of amenity migration in future research could validate the total extent of the "access to mountain recreation and urban amenities" (R3) archetype.

## Limitations

A longstanding difficulty with archetype analysis and demographic research is choosing a scale of analysis. We selected the county as our unit of analysis because it was the smallest unit possible in Census of Agriculture data, which we needed to describe agricultural change. However, our study area has counties of very different sizes, some of which are very large. Large counties may actually contain dynamics of multiple archetypes, which we are not able to capture when using the county as a base unit. For example, Owyhee County, the largest in our study area, was assigned the most rural archetype where farmland is least threatened by development (R5-A5), yet our preliminary qualitative data shows that the northern part of the county is experiencing the effects of urban sprawl from bordering Ada County [R1-A1, @daumale2026]. Qualitative social science is critical for both validating the usefulness of archetypes and revealing important nuance in larger geographical areas.

## Future Directions

In this analysis, we reveal the spatial and temporal arrangement of different social-ecological-agricultural contexts and validate some of those archetypes with qualitative data. The identification of these archetypes is a first step towards understanding and mitigating farmland loss in this area. First, more research is needed to identify successful and unsuccessful adaptations to these agricultural changes at both the farm and local governance scale, so that future policies for certain archetypes can be informed by outcomes in the same archetype. Next, characterization of spatial patterns of land use change within each archetype is needed to improve upon land use change models that focus solely on urban sprawl as an agricultural conversion mechanism. Finally, more inestigation is needed regarding the additional, unexpected resource archetype we identified (R4 - agriculture further from urban and recreational amenities), particularly an understanding of its range of validity and its potentially unique social and agricultural changes compared to other, more well understood archetypes of agricultural change.

# Conclusions

We used a mixed methods archetypes approach to identify recurring patterns of social-ecological subsystems across space and time in a region of the western US where agricultural lands are at risk of conversion. We identified five resource types and five actor types among the study area counties between 1990 and 2020. Resource archetypes were strongly influenced by developed land, housing density, land near major roadways, and federal land, while actors archetypes were strongly influenced by geographical isolation and population density. We found that multiple archetypes of resource systems were at risk of farmland loss, but these risks were mediated by actor archetypes, with some actor types associated with more development than others. The quantitative clusters indicated some archetypes clearly associated with one process of farmland loss (i.e. R1, R3) and other archetypes potentially associated with multiple processes (i.e. R2, R4) or none of these processes (R5). Using interview data, we were able to validate some of these archetypes, matching them with cases of urban sprawl, amenity migration, and agricultural industrialization. Resource archetypes rarely shifted through time, but actor archetype shifts across the study period revealed a progression by which population growth and urbanization drives counties to transition to more urban actors archetypes. On a regional scale, this work reveals counties with similar resources and actors, and further qualitative work can reveal farmland protection strategies that these similar counties may successfully share. This work advances archetype analysis by validating quantitative clusters with qualitative interview data and implementing dynamic archetype analysis in a study period with gradual social change instead of more sudden policy change.

# Main Takeaways

## Farmlands are threatened by more than urban growth

The original inspiration for this dissertation chapter was the observation that farmland loss prediction models underestimate farmland loss that isn't associated with urban growth. This analysis, and especially archetype R1, show that the average condition for this study area is farmland loss in places without large urban areas.

The presence of A1 actors (educated, growing, urban population) is associated with changes in resource systems, even if no counties transitioned from one resource archetype to another. Counties with A1 actors tend to accelerate their developed land growth and housing density. However, A1 does not always mean accelerated development, as evidenced by Blaine County, which has had wealthy inhabitants for a long time and has implemented land protections so that their resource system more closely matches more isolated counties.
